opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think explainable AI is really exciting for biology and health care because it changes what we can do with machine learning models. It isn't only about trusting a prediction. It's about learning something new from the model.

For a long time the focus was accuracy: can we predict whether a patient will develop a complication, or whether a cancer will respond to a drug? Those models are powerful, but if you can't see why they make a prediction, you can't turn it into biological insight or clinical action. Explainability methods, especially principled feature attribution approaches like Shapley value–based methods, let us ask which features drove a prediction, for this specific patient or sample.

That opens several directions. The first is scientific discovery. In cancer pharmacogenomics, for example, we can train models on gene expression data to predict drug response. Explaining those models then points us to genes or pathways that seem to drive sensitivity or resistance. That generates hypotheses biologists can test in the lab, and it can suggest drug combinations or biomarkers people wouldn't have thought to look at.

The second is clinical decision support. In anesthesiology, we worked on predicting hypoxemia during surgery. A bare risk score isn't very useful to an anesthesiologist. If you also show which factors are driving the risk right now, like oxygen saturation trends, tidal volume, or the patient's BMI, the clinician can act on it. And explanations can sometimes reveal patterns clinicians didn't fully appreciate.

The third, which I think is underappreciated, is auditing AI models themselves. When we explained dermatology classifiers or chest X-ray models for COVID-19, we found they often relied on shortcuts. They used things like text markers, image artifacts, or hospital-specific features rather than real pathology. Explainability becomes a tool for checking whether a model learned medicine or just learned the dataset. That's essential before anything gets deployed.

Finally, there's a feedback loop with the methods themselves. Biological data is high-dimensional, with correlated features and complex interactions. That pushes us to develop better explanation methods: ones that handle correlated genes, explain at the level of pathways or concepts rather than single features, and scale to very large models. So biology isn't just an application area for explainable AI. It's driving new research in explainable AI itself.

To me, the biggest shift is that the model becomes a lens on the data. It's no longer just a black box that outputs a number.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, explainable AI in biology and health care is less about satisfying a regulator who wants to see why a model made a prediction, and more about using the model as a scientific instrument. In a lot of other domains, the question is "can I trust this prediction?" In biology, the question is "what did the model learn about the underlying system that I didn't already know?"

So take something like gene expression data from cancer patients. You can train a model to predict drug response, and it might do that reasonably well. But if you can then ask the model, feature by feature, which genes it's relying on and how those contributions interact, you now have hypotheses about mechanism. Those are things a biologist can take back to the bench and actually test. The explanation becomes the output, not a side product.

That's what motivated a lot of our work on SHAP and feature attribution more broadly. The idea is that you want a principled way to say how much each input contributed to a prediction, with some mathematical guarantees so that different people looking at the same model get a consistent answer. Once you have that, you can start to aggregate explanations across thousands of samples and see patterns, and those patterns start to look like biology.

In the clinical setting, the direction I find most exciting is what you might call explainable prediction in real time. We did work on anesthesia, predicting hypoxemia during surgery, and the model was good at the prediction, but what actually changed the conversation with the anesthesiologists was that it could tell them which signals were driving the risk right now. That's a different kind of tool. It supports the clinician's own reasoning rather than replacing it, and it also lets them catch when the model is relying on something spurious.

And that last point opens a research direction on its own. When you look at explanations systematically, you discover shortcuts, batch effects, confounding by the hospital or the sequencing platform, all sorts of things. Interpretability becomes a kind of auditing tool for datasets, not just models. I think that's going to matter more and more as the datasets get larger and messier.

So to summarize, I'd say three directions. First, explanations as a hypothesis-generation engine for discovering mechanism. Second, explanations as a way to put AI into the clinical loop in a form that humans can actually act on. And third, explanations as a lens for understanding and cleaning the data itself. All three are pretty different from the way explainability is typically framed, and all three feel wide open to me.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most exciting possibilities is using explainable AI to generate scientific hypotheses. In biology and health care, we often train a model to predict something—whether a patient has a disease, for example. But the scientific question goes beyond whether that prediction is accurate. We want to understand what the model has learned and whether it can reveal something about the underlying biology.

Imagine a model that predicts disease from gene expression data. If we can understand which genes, or combinations of genes, contribute to its predictions, we can identify patterns to investigate experimentally. That creates a connection between predictive modeling and biological discovery.

Of course, explaining a model’s prediction does not establish causality. A model might use a signal that reflects how the data were collected rather than a disease mechanism. So explanations can also help us examine those possibilities and decide what needs further validation.

For me, that opens a research direction where we don’t stop at building an accurate model. We use it to ask better questions, design experiments, and ultimately learn something new about disease.

sol-6.1.text:
I see explainable AI as a way to turn predictive models into tools for scientific discovery. In biology and health care, we often build a model to predict an outcome—whether someone has a disease, for example. But the next question is, what has the model learned? Which genes, molecular processes, or clinical features contribute to that prediction? And can understanding those contributions help us ask a new biological question?

That creates a really interesting research loop. We train a model, use explanations to identify potentially meaningful patterns, and then take those patterns back to domain experts for further investigation. An explanation doesn’t establish causality, but it can suggest hypotheses that we can test experimentally.

It also opens questions about the models themselves. A model might perform well because it captures disease biology, or because it picks up differences in how the data were collected. Understanding that distinction is essential if we want these systems to be useful in health care. So, for me, explainable AI is both a way to scrutinize predictions and a way to generate new scientific questions.
